fanoutqa_039373.x:
Philip H. Dybvig :: Career :: chunk_0001
Dybvig attended [Indiana University](/wiki/Indiana_University "Indiana University") and received in 1976 a BA in mathematics and physics. He then attended the economics PhD program at [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") for one year before transferring to [Yale University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), where he received the MA (1978), MPhil (1978), and PhD (1979) degrees in economics.[[3]](#cite_note-CV-3) His thesis, titled "Recovering additive utility functions", was supervised by [Stephen A. Ross](/wiki/Stephen_A._Ross "Stephen A. Ross").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Dybvig specializes in [asset pricing](/wiki/Asset_pricing "Asset pricing"), banking, investments, and [corporate governance](/wiki/Corporate_governance "Corporate governance").[[5]](#cite_note-Olin_Faculty-5) He was formerly a professor at [Yale University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), and assistant professor at [Princeton University](/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University").

Dybvig was president of the [Western Finance Association](/wiki/Western_Finance_Association "Western Finance Association") from 2002 to 2003, and was director of the Institute of Financial Studies at [Southwestern University of Finance and Economics](/wiki/Southwestern_University_of_Finance_and_Economics "Southwestern University of Finance and Economics") ([Chengdu](/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), [PRC](/wiki/PRC "PRC")) from 2010 to 2021. He has been editor or associate editor of multiple journals, including the *Journal of Economic Theory*, *Finance and Stochastics*, *Journal of Finance*, *Journal of Financial Intermediation*, *Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis*, and *Review of Financial Studies*.[[3]](#cite_note-CV-3)

Dybvig is known for his work with [Douglas Diamond](/wiki/Douglas_Diamond "Douglas Diamond") on the [Diamond–Dybvig model](/wiki/Diamond%E2%80%93Dybvig_model "Diamond–Dybvig model") of bank runs.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

Dybvig was awarded the 2022 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences"),

fanoutqa_001997.t: Lung cancer :: Signs and symptoms :: chunk_0002
fanoutqa_001997.x:
Lung cancer :: Signs and symptoms :: chunk_0002
Early lung cancer often has no symptoms. When symptoms do arise they are often [nonspecific](/wiki/Signs_and_symptoms#Nonspecific_symptoms "Signs and symptoms") respiratory problems – [coughing](/wiki/Cough "Cough"), [shortness of breath](/wiki/Shortness_of_breath "Shortness of breath"), or [chest pain](/wiki/Chest_pain "Chest pain") – that can differ from person to person.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-6) Those who experience coughing tend to report either a new cough, or an increase in the frequency or strength of a pre-existing cough.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-6) Around one in four [cough up blood](/wiki/Hemoptysis "Hemoptysis"), ranging from small streaks in the [sputum](/wiki/Sputum "Sputum") to large amounts.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENasimSabathEapen2019"Clinical_Manifestations"-7)[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-6) Around half of those diagnosed with lung cancer experience shortness of breath, while 25–50% experience a dull, persistent chest pain that remains in the same location over time.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-6) In addition to respiratory symptoms, some experience [systemic symptoms](/wiki/Systemic_disease "Systemic disease") including [loss of appetite](/wiki/Anorexia_(symptom) "Anorexia (symptom)"), [weight loss](/wiki/Weight_loss "Weight loss"), general weakness, [fever](/wiki/Fever "Fever"), and [night sweats](/wiki/Night_sweats "Night sweats").[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPastisGonzalezSilvestri2022"Presentation/Initial_Evaluation"-6)[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHornIams2022"Clinical_Manifestations"-8)

Some less common symptoms suggest tumors in particular locations. Tumors in the [thorax](/wiki/Thorax "Thorax") can cause breathing problems by obstructing the [trachea](/wiki/Trachea "Trachea") or disrupting the nerve to the [diaphragm](/wiki/Thoracic_diaphragm "Thoracic diaphragm"); [difficulty swallowing](/wiki/Dysphagia "Dysphagia") by compressing the [esophagus](/wiki/Esophagus "

fanoutqa_031693.x:
Case Closed :: Reception :: Popularity :: Sales :: chunk_0010
By October 2021, the *Case Closed* manga had over 250 million copies in circulation worldwide, making it one of the [best-selling manga series](/wiki/List_of_best-selling_manga "List of best-selling manga"),[[120]](#cite_note-122) having been sold in 25 countries.[[121]](#cite_note-cnc-123) By January 2023, the manga had over 270 million copies in circulation worldwide.[[122]](#cite_note-124)[[123]](#cite_note-125) In Japan, individual volumes frequently appear on the lists of best-selling manga.[[124]](#cite_note-126)[[125]](#cite_note-127) *Case Closed* was the nineteenth best selling manga in 2011, with 2,120,091 copies sold.[[126]](#cite_note-128) *Nikkei Entertainment* magazine published a list of top 50 manga creators by sales since January 2010, in its September 2011 issue; Gosho Aoyama, the author of *Case Closed* was ranked sixteenth, with 3,320,000 copies sold.[[127]](#cite_note-129) It was the seventeenth best selling manga in 2012, with 2,430,572 copies sold.[[128]](#cite_note-130) In 2013, *Case Closed* became the 24th best selling manga, with 1,966,206 copies sold.[[129]](#cite_note-131) In 2024, alongside *[Space Brothers](/wiki/Space_Brothers_(manga) "Space Brothers (manga)")*, *Case Closed* won the grand prize of [Rakuten Kobo](/wiki/Kobo_Inc. "Kobo Inc.")'s second E-book Award in the "Long Seller Comic" category.[[130]](#cite_note-132)

Licensed merchandise based on *Detective Conan* are sold in Asia. In Japan, *Detective Conan* licensed merchandise sold ¥2.89 billion in 2003, ¥17.29 billion during 2005–2008, and ¥9.03 billion during 2010–2012, adding up to at least ¥29.21 billion ($366.08 million) sold in Japan between 2003 and 2012.[[131]](#cite_note-charabiz-133) The first volume of *Case Closed* appeared thrice in the top ten selling lists, right after its premiere,[[132]](#cite_note-134) the same volume has also appeared in the [Diamond Comic Distributors](/wiki/Diamond_Comic_Distributors "Diamond Comic Distributors")'s ranking list.[[133]](#cite_note-135) Later-published volumes have appeared on [*The New York Times* Manga Best Sellers](/wiki/List_of_The_New_York_Times_Manga_Be

After Nehru [died](/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Jawaharlal_Nehru "Death and state funeral of Jawaharlal Nehru") in office in May 1964, [Lal Bahadur Shastri](/wiki/Lal_Bahadur_Shastri "Lal Bahadur Shastri") was unanimously chosen by the Congress to be parliamentary leader, and thus prime minister. After the [India–Pakistan war of 1965](/wiki/India%E2%80%93Pakistan_war_of_1965 "India–Pakistan war of 1965"), Shastri [died](/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Lal_Bahadur_Shastri "Death and state funeral of Lal Bahadur Shastri") in January 1966, soon after signing the [Tashkent Peace Declaration](/wiki/Tashkent_Declaration "Tashkent Declaration"). The Congress chose [Indira Gandhi](/wiki/Indira_Gandhi "Indira Gandhi") to be prime minister. She led the party to election victories in [1967](/wiki/1967_Indian_general_election "1967 Indian general election") and [1971](/wiki/1971_Indian_general_election "1971 Indian general election"), the latter a [landslide](/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") after Pakistan's defeat in the [Bangladesh Liberation War](/wiki/Bangladesh_Liberation_War "Bangladesh Liberation War"). In 1975, Indira Gandhi declared a [state of emergency](/wiki/The_Emergency_(India) "The Emergency (India)"), suspending many civil liberties. See also: [List of megathrust earthquakes](/wiki/List_of_megathrust_earthquakes "List of megathrust earthquakes")

Great earthquakes such as the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake are generally associated with [megathrust](/wiki/Megathrust_earthquake "Megathrust earthquake") events in [subduction](/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") zones. Their [seismic moments](/wiki/Seismic_moment "Seismic moment") can account for a significant fraction of the global seismic moment across century-scale periods. Of all the moment released by earthquakes in the 100 years from 1906 through 2005, roughly one-eighth was due to the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake.[[35]](#cite_note-:0-36) This quake, together with the [Great Alaskan earthquake](/wiki/1964_Alaska_earthquake "1964 Alaska earthquake") (1964) and the [Great Chilean earthquake](/wiki/1960_Valdivia_earthquake "1960 Valdivia earthquake") (1960), account for almost half of the total moment.[[35]](#cite_note-:0-36)[[36]](#cite_note-37)

Since 1900, the only earthquakes recorded with a greater magnitude were the 1960 Chile earthquake (magnitude 9.5) and the 1964 Alaska earthquake in [Prince William Sound](/wiki/Prince_William_Sound "Prince William Sound") (magnitude 9.2). The only other recorded earthquakes of magnitude 9.0 or greater were off [Kamchatka, Russia, in November 1952](/wiki/1952_Severo-Kurilsk_earthquake "1952 Severo-Kurilsk earthquake") (magnitude 9.0) and [Tōhoku, Japan, in March 2011](/wiki/2011_T%C5%8Dhoku_earthquake_and_tsunami "2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami") (magnitude 9.1). Each of these megathrust earthquakes also spawned tsunamis in the Pacific Ocean. In comparison to the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake, the death toll from these earthquakes and tsunamis was significantly lower, primarily because of the lower population density along the coasts near affected areas.[[8]](#cite_note-:1-8)

The Football Association Premier League Ltd (FAPL)[[64]](#cite_note-66)[[65]](#cite_note-67)[[66]](#cite_note-68) is operated as a corporation and is owned by the 20 member clubs. Each club is a [shareholder](/wiki/Shareholder "Shareholder"), with one vote each on issues such as rule changes and contracts. The clubs select a chairman, chief executive, and board of directors to oversee the daily operations of the league.[[67]](#cite_note-69) The Football Association is not directly involved in the day-to-day operations of the Premier League, but has veto power as a special shareholder during the election of the chairman and chief executive and when new rules are adopted by the league.[[68]](#cite_note-70)

The current chief executive is [Richard Masters](/wiki/Richard_Masters_(football) "Richard Masters (football)"), who was appointed in December 2019.[[69]](#cite_note-71) The chair is currently [Alison Brittain](/wiki/Alison_Brittain "Alison Brittain"), who took over the role in early 2023.[[70]](#cite_note-72)

The Premier League sends representatives to UEFA's [European Club Association](/wiki/European_Club_Association "European Club Association"), the number of clubs and the clubs themselves chosen according to [UEFA coefficients](/wiki/UEFA_coefficient "UEFA coefficient"). The **Henley Passport Index** is an annual global ranking of countries according to the travel freedom allowed by those countries' ordinary [passports](/wiki/Passports "Passports") for their citizens.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) The index was created by Christian Kälin[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) and launched in 2005 as [Henley & Partners](/wiki/Henley_%26_Partners "Henley & Partners") [Visa](/wiki/Travel_visa "Travel visa") Restrictions Index.[[7]](#cite_note-tertiary_source_1-7) Its name was changed to Henley Passport Index in January 2018.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The index is updated on a quarterly basis to reflect changes in global visa policies.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

The index annually ranks 199 passports of the world by the number of countries that their holders can travel to without requiring a visa.[[10]](#cite_note-annual_ranking-10) The number of countries that a specific passport can access becomes its visa-free "score". The data is obtained from the [International Air Transport Association](/wiki/International_Air_Transport_Association "International Air Transport Association") (IATA)'s[[11]](#cite_note-11) [Timatic](/wiki/Timatic "Timatic") documentation requirements database.[[7]](#cite_note-tertiary_source_1-7)[[12]](#cite_note-12)

The United Kingdom's topography

[England](/wiki/Geography_of_England "Geography of England") accounts for 53 per cent of the UK, covering 50,350 square miles (130,395 km2).[[147]](#cite_note-165) Most of the country consists of lowland terrain,[[148]](#cite_note-Atlapedia-166) with upland and mountainous terrain northwest of the [Tees–Exe line](/wiki/Tees%E2%80%93Exe_line "Tees–Exe line") which roughly divides the UK into [lowland and upland](/wiki/Lowland_and_upland "Lowland and upland") areas. Lowland areas include [Cornwall](/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall"), the [New Forest](/wiki/New_Forest "New Forest"), the [South Downs](/wiki/South_Downs "South Downs") and the [Norfolk Broads](/wiki/The_Broads "The Broads"). Upland areas include the [Lake District](/wiki/Lake_District "Lake District"), the [Pennines](/wiki/Pennines "Pennines"), the [Yorkshire Dales](/wiki/Yorkshire_Dales "Yorkshire Dales"), [Exmoor](/wiki/Exmoor "Exmoor") and [Dartmoor](/wiki/Dartmoor "Dartmoor"). The main rivers and estuaries are the [Thames](/wiki/River_Thames "River Thames"), [Severn](/wiki/River_Severn "River Severn"), and the [Humber](/wiki/Humber "Humber"). England's highest mountain is [Scafell Pike](/wiki/Scafell_Pike "Scafell Pike"), at 978 metres (3,209 ft) in the Lake District; its largest island is the [Isle of Wight](/wiki/Isle_of_Wight "Isle of Wight").

[Scotland](/wiki/Geography_of_Scotland "Geography of Scotland") accounts for 32 per cent of the UK, covering 30,410 square miles (78,772 km2).[[149]](#cite_note-167) This includes [nearly 800 islands](/wiki/List_of_islands_of_Scotland "List of islands of Scotland"),[[150]](#cite_note-168) notably the [Hebrides](/wiki/Hebrides "Hebrides"), [Orkney](/wiki/Orkney "Orkney") Islands and [Shetland Islands](/wiki/Shetland_Islands "Shetland Islands"). Scotland is the most mountainous constituent country of the UK. The United States has hosted the modern Olympic Games eight times, more than any other nation. These occasions span from the 1904 St. Louis Olympics to the 2002 Salt Lake City Winter Olympics. Beyond hosting, the U.S. has significantly impacted the Olympics through athletic achievements, innovations in sports infrastructure and technology, and cultural contributions. Its influence extends to advocating Olympic ideals and leaving lasting legacies in host cities. Overall, the U.S. plays a central role in the history and ongoing development of the Olympic movement. For example, the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics pioneered the use of electronic timing devices. The 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, for instance, set new standards for opening and closing ceremonies. Even when not hosting, the U.S. has played a crucial role in the administration and promotion of the Olympics through organizations like the [United States Olympic Committee](/wiki/United_States_Olympic_Committee "United States Olympic Committee") (USOC) and its participation in the [International Olympic Committee](/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC). Alain Aspect :: Distinctions :: chunk_0003
Aspect was elected a [Foreign Member of the Royal Society](/wiki/List_of_Fellows_of_the_Royal_Society_elected_in_2015 "List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 2015") (ForMemRS) in 2015.[[15]](#cite_note-15) His certificate of election reads:

> For his fundamental experiments in quantum optics and atomic physics. Alain Aspect was the first to exclude subluminal communication between the measurement stations in experimental demonstrations that quantum mechanics invalidates separable hidden-variable theories and the first to demonstrate experimentally the wave–particle duality of single photons. He co-invented the technique of velocity-selective coherent population trapping, was the first to compare the [Hanbury Brown-Twiss](/wiki/Hanbury_Brown_and_Twiss_effect "Hanbury Brown and Twiss effect") correlations of fermions and bosons under the same conditions, and the first to demonstrate Anderson localization in an ultra-cold atom system. His experiments illuminate fundamental aspects of the quantum-mechanical behaviour of single photons, photon pairs and atoms.[[1]](#cite_note-royal-1)

In 2005 he was awarded the gold medal of the [Centre national de la recherche scientifique](/wiki/Centre_national_de_la_recherche_scientifique "Centre national de la recherche scientifique"), where he is Research Director. The 2010 [Wolf Prize](/wiki/Wolf_Prize "Wolf Prize") in physics was awarded to Aspect, [Anton Zeilinger](/wiki/Anton_Zeilinger "Anton Zeilinger") and [John Clauser](/wiki/John_Clauser "John Clauser"). In 2013 Aspect was awarded both the [Niels Bohr International Gold Medal](/wiki/Niels_Bohr_International_Gold_Medal "Niels Bohr International Gold Medal") and the [UNESCO Niels Bohr Medal](/wiki/UNESCO_Niels_Bohr_Medal "UNESCO Niels Bohr Medal"). In 2011, he was assigned the [Medal of the City of Paris](/wiki/Medal_of_the_City_of_Paris "Medal of the City of Paris"). In 2013, he was also awarded the [Balzan Prize](/wiki/Balzan_Prize "Balzan Prize") for Quantum Information Processing and Communication. In 2014, he was named Officer of the [Legion of Honour](/wiki/Legion_of_Honour "Legion of Honour").[[16]](#cite_note-16
